To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
genetic algorithms are not good at forecasting.
genetic-based learning classifier do not outperform simple forecasting algorithms and that this is due to the fact that they are not converging.

(1) genetic-based learning classifier algorithms, as currently implemented, are not a promising alternative to standard forecasting methods in financial markets; (2) the use of such algorithms in agent-based computational finance to represent agents process for expectations formation, as it is currently done in the literature, may not be a plausible approach.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how well the algorithm performs in the context of a forecast evaluation exercise, and how this performance is affected when we make its key parameters endogenously.
the issue of whether a genetic-based learning algorithm can beat simple forecasting algorithms.
the use of genetic algorithms in the context of agent-based computational finance, and it is a step towards the integration of agent-based computational methods with econometric methods.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of genetic based learning classifier systems as a forecasting device is not supported by empirical results.
, at the current state of the art, genetic-based learning classifier algorithms cannot be used as forecasting devices, neither in a real world nor in an agent-based simulation.

the use of a genetic-based learning system in forecasting is an empirical case against the usefulness of genetic-based learning systems as forecasting devices, and, consequently, against the usefulness of such systems in representing agent expectations formation in the context of agent-based computational finance models.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in order to be useful as forecasting devices, the learning classifier systems must be made to converge to some stable state and, in order for them to do so, the algorithm parameters must be made endogenous.

genetic-based learning classifier should be considered as a tool for forecasting only when the researcher has a very good understanding of the problem at hand and when there is a strong theoretical reason to believe that the algorithm should perform better than simpler ones.
, if the aim is to build an algorithm capable of forecasting stock returns better than a random walk, then the use of genetic learning classifier systems does not seem to be the way to go.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the performance of a genetic-based learning algorithm is highly sensitive to the choice of its parameters.
the use of a genetic-based learning algorithm in forecasting stock returns does not necessarily lead to a superior performance.

, in the context of financial forecasting, it is not clear how the genetic-based learning algorithm can be made to converge to a reasonable forecasting device, and that this issue is likely to remain unsolved as long as the algorithm is kept in the form presented by the original authors.
